The hip radiograph is one of the highest-yield films in acute medicine: an elderly patient falls, cannot weight-bear, and the leg lies shortened and externally rotated. Your job is to confirm a neck of femur (NOF) fracture, classify it, and recognise when a normal-looking film must not reassure you.

1Always demand two views
Request an AP pelvis plus a lateral of the affected hip. A fracture can be all but invisible on one projection and obvious on the other, so a single AP is never enough. The AP lets you compare both hips side-by-side; the lateral reveals posterior displacement and dislocation. Assess bone (trabeculae, cortex), joint space, and — critically — the position of the limb.
📷 Image placeholder — AP pelvis showing a displaced left subcapital NOF fracture: the femoral head sits medially, the neck is foreshortened, and the affected leg is externally rotated (lesser trochanter prominent).
2Trace Shenton's line
Shenton's line is the smooth continuous curve running along the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus onto the inferomedial border of the femoral neck. In a normal hip it is an unbroken arc. Any break or step in this curve signals a fractured neck of femur or a hip dislocation. Loss of the line is often the first sign your eye catches.
Step or disruption in Shenton's line→fractured NOF or hip dislocation until proven otherwise
Disrupted or angulated trabecular lines crossing the femoral neck
Cortical break, buckle, or step in the smooth femoral neck outline
Shortened, externally rotated limb — lesser trochanter unusually prominent
3Classify: intracapsular vs extracapsular
The capsule attaches along the intertrochanteric line, so where the fracture sits relative to it decides the blood-supply risk and the operation. Intracapsular fractures (subcapital, transcervical) disrupt the retrograde supply from the medial femoral circumflex artery, threatening avascular necrosis (AVN) and non-union. Extracapsular fractures (intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric) spare that supply, so the head can safely be retained.
🩸Intracapsular (displaced)
Subcapital/transcervical, Garden III–IV. Blood supply lost → AVN risk. Replace the head: hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement (THR) in fit, mobile patients.
🔩Intracapsular (undisplaced)
Garden I–II. Supply likely intact, so preserve the head: internal fixation with cannulated screws.
🔧Intertrochanteric
Extracapsular, supply preserved. Fix with a dynamic hip screw (DHS), allowing controlled compression at the fracture.
🔗Subtrochanteric
Extracapsular, below the trochanters. Stabilise with an intramedullary nail.
4The Garden classification
Applied to intracapsular fractures: I incomplete/impacted (valgus), II complete but undisplaced, III complete with partial displacement, IV complete with full displacement. A useful shorthand: Garden I–II are undisplaced (fix), III–IV are displaced (replace).
5Don't miss the other pathologies
Osteoarthritis — joint space narrowing, marginal osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts. AVN — patchy sclerosis and the subchondral crescent sign, later femoral head collapse. Pathological fracture / metastases — a lytic or sclerotic lesion at the fracture site (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid). Hip dislocation — usually posterior, limb flexed/adducted/internally rotated, head lying superolaterally; common in prosthetic hips. In children think Perthes and SUFE (assessed separately).
📷 Image placeholder — AP pelvis of hip osteoarthritis for contrast: superior joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes at the acetabular margin, and a subchondral cyst in the femoral head.
🚩 A clinically suspected NOF fracture — hip pain, unable to weight-bear, shortened and externally rotated leg — with a NORMAL X-ray is not cleared. An occult fracture may be radiographically invisible. Proceed to MRI (most sensitive) or CT before discharge. Missing one is a devastating error.
🎓 A NOF fracture is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in the elderly. Treat it as a systemic event, not just a bone: prompt orthogeriatric co-management, effective analgesia (consider a fascia iliaca block), and surgery within 36 hours of admission all improve survival and functional recovery.

A femur X-ray is the workhorse film for thigh trauma, but the golden rule is that a single femur is never enough — you must always image the joint above and the joint below. That means a full-length AP and lateral femur that includes the hip AND the knee, because associated hip fractures/dislocations and knee injuries are easily missed on a shaft-only view. In the young a shaft fracture usually means high-energy trauma; in the elderly or after trivial force, think pathological or atypical fracture — and never forget that a closed femoral shaft fracture can hide over a litre of blood.

📷 Image placeholder — AP full-length femur radiograph showing a mid-shaft transverse fracture with shortening; ensure both the hip and knee joints are included on the film.
1Check the film is adequate
Confirm two views (AP and lateral) and that both the hip and the knee are visible. A shaft fracture with a normal-looking proximal femur may still have an ipsilateral femoral neck fracture — hence "image the joint above and below."
2Describe the fracture systematically
State the site (proximal/subtrochanteric, mid-shaft/diaphyseal, distal/supracondylar), pattern (transverse, spiral, comminuted, segmental), displacement, shortening and angulation. A clear description drives management and communication with orthopaedics.
Transverse + comminuted mid-shaft in a young RTC patient → high-energy injury.
Distal supracondylar fracture → assess for popliteal artery injury and intra-articular knee extension.
Elderly or minimal-trauma fracture→suspect a PATHOLOGICAL fracture — the femur is the commonest long bone for metastases (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid) or myeloma; look for a lytic lesion at the fracture site.
3Spot the ATYPICAL femoral fracture
A subtrochanteric or diaphyseal transverse fracture with lateral cortical beaking/thickening, associated with long-term bisphosphonate use. It is often bilateral and preceded by weeks of prodromal thigh pain — always X-ray the contralateral femur.
📷 Image placeholder — atypical femoral fracture: transverse subtrochanteric lucency with focal lateral cortical beaking and thickening in a patient on long-term bisphosphonates.
🩸Haemorrhage
~1–1.5 L blood loss per closed femoral shaft fracture; bilateral fractures can cause hypovolaemic shock.
🫁Fat embolism
Respiratory distress, petechiae and confusion 24–72 h after a long-bone fracture.
🦴Pathological cause
Minimal trauma → metastasis or myeloma; the femur is the commonest long bone for mets.
💊Atypical fracture
Transverse subtrochanteric/diaphyseal fracture with lateral beaking on long-term bisphosphonates.
4Manage the patient, not just the film
ABCDE with resuscitation and IV access; adequate analgesia (including a femoral nerve block); apply a Thomas splint / traction to a shaft fracture to reduce blood loss, pain and further soft-tissue injury; then definitive fixation with an intramedullary nail (or plate for some distal fractures). Check distal neurovascular status before and after splinting.
🚩 A femoral shaft fracture is a resuscitation problem: assess for haemorrhagic shock and activate the major haemorrhage protocol if needed. An open fracture or one with neurovascular compromise (absent distal, femoral or popliteal pulses) is a surgical emergency. Watch for fat embolism at 24–72 h, and always consider a pathological or atypical cause when trauma is minimal.
🎓 Two habits pass exams and protect patients: always image the joint above and below (a shaft film without the hip and knee is incomplete), and always ask "why did this bone break?" — trivial force in an older patient means metastasis, myeloma or a bisphosphonate-related atypical fracture until proven otherwise.

The knee X-ray is a bread-and-butter A&E film. Two rules save you: image the right patients (Ottawa knee rules), and never miss the subtle signs of an intra-articular fracture — above all the fat–fluid level of a lipohaemarthrosis, which betrays a fracture you may not actually see. Standard series is an AP and a lateral; add a horizontal-beam lateral if you suspect a fluid level, and weight-bearing views for osteoarthritis.

1Who to image — Ottawa knee rules

X-ray a knee injury only if one or more of these is present, otherwise a fracture is very unlikely:

Age ≥55 OR isolated patellar tenderness OR tenderness at the fibular head OR cannot flex to 90° OR cannot weight-bear 4 steps (both immediately and in the ED)→Image the knee (AP + lateral)

None of these → clinically clear, no film needed. These rules are highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures.

2The lipohaemarthrosis / fat–fluid level

On a horizontal-beam lateral the film catches fluid layering under gravity. Marrow fat released by a fracture floats on top of blood in the suprapatellar recess, producing a straight fat–fluid level. This is a strong sign of an intra-articular fracture — classically a subtle tibial plateau fracture — even when no fracture line is visible.

Horizontal line in the suprapatellar recess = fat–fluid level = blood + marrow fat in the joint.
A supine AP or standard lateral can hide it — you need the beam horizontal to see the layering.
No visible fracture line does not exclude one; the fat came from somewhere.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: horizontal-beam lateral knee showing a fat–fluid level in the suprapatellar recess (lipohaemarthrosis).
3Fractures & avulsions to name
🦴Tibial plateau
Split/depression of the (usually lateral) plateau; Schatzker classification; often subtle — CT for depression.
🔻Patella
Transverse from direct blow/quads pull; check patella alta/baja and straight-leg-raise. Don't call a smooth-margined superolateral bipartite patella a fracture.
✂️Segond
Small avulsion off the lateral tibial condyle — highly associated with ACL rupture.
⛰️Tibial spine avulsion
Avulsed intercondylar eminence — the ACL's bony equivalent, common in children.
🔩Fibular head avulsion
Arcuate sign — biceps femoris / arcuate complex avulsion, posterolateral corner injury.
Displaced patella / large effusion on the lateral view→Joint effusion — inspect hard for an occult intra-articular fracture
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: AP knee showing a Segond fracture (thin cortical avulsion off the lateral tibial condyle) with adjacent lateral plateau.
4Osteoarthritis

The chronic knee: look for medial joint space narrowing (loss preferentially medial), marginal osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts. Assess on weight-bearing views — a supine film underestimates joint-space loss because the compartment is unloaded.

🚩 A lipohaemarthrosis is an intra-articular fracture until proven otherwise → CT/further imaging. Extensor mechanism disruption (patellar fracture, unable to straight-leg-raise) needs orthopaedics. A knee dislocation (rare, high-energy) is a vascular emergency — popliteal artery injury: check distal pulses / ABPI and get CT angiography even if the knee has spontaneously reduced.
🎓 If you see fat floating on blood, don't relax because the bones "look intact" — the fluid level is the diagnosis. Hunt for a tibial plateau fracture and lower your threshold to CT.

The tibia and fibula are best imaged as a full-length AP and lateral radiograph that includes both the knee and the ankle joint. The two bones form a bony ring bridged by the proximal and distal tib-fib joints, so an isolated fracture of one bone should always prompt a search for injury at the joint at the other end — a solitary fibular fracture, for example, may be the visible clue to a serious ankle disruption.

1Image the whole bone — knee AND ankle
A tibial radiograph that stops short of a joint is inadequate. Because the tib-fib complex behaves mechanically like a ring, force applied at one point is often transmitted to the far end. Always confirm the film includes the joint above and below and inspect each carefully.
Isolated fracture of one bone (e.g. proximal fibula)→actively hunt for a paired injury at the opposite joint
AP + lateral, full length
Knee joint included
Ankle mortise included
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: full-length AP tibia/fibula showing the knee at the top and the ankle mortise at the bottom, demonstrating an adequate view of the whole ring.
2Tibial shaft fracture — the classic open long bone
The tibia is the commonest long bone to sustain an open fracture. Its anteromedial (subcutaneous) border lies immediately beneath thin skin with poor overlying muscle, so displaced fragments readily breach the skin, giving a high rate of open injuries and poor soft-tissue coverage. Always inspect the whole limb for wounds, however small.
Any wound near a tibial fracture→treat as open until proven otherwise
3Maisonneuve fracture — proximal fibula + ankle
A Maisonneuve fracture is a fracture of the proximal fibula combined with an ankle injury: a medial malleolar fracture or deltoid ligament rupture plus disruption of the syndesmosis and interosseous membrane. The ankle film may look almost normal, so in any ankle injury with medial-side tenderness, examine and image the whole length of the fibula up to the knee.
Ankle injury + medial malleolar tenderness, no lateral malleolar fracture→palpate and X-ray the proximal fibula
4Describe the fracture systematically
Characterise the pattern (transverse, spiral, oblique, comminuted or segmental), then displacement, angulation and shortening. Spiral patterns imply a twisting mechanism; segmental and comminuted patterns imply high energy. Stress fractures in athletes and soldiers may be very subtle — a faint lucency or a hint of periosteal reaction — and are often invisible on the initial film.
📏Transverse
Direct/bending force, horizontal line
🌀Spiral
Twisting force, oblique curving line
💥Comminuted
≥3 fragments, high energy
🪵Segmental
Two levels, isolated middle segment
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph: a mid-shaft tibial spiral fracture with an associated proximal fibular fracture, illustrating the ring principle and the need to describe pattern, displacement and angulation.
🚩 The tibia is the classic site for acute compartment syndrome. Suspect it with pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the toes; the late 'P's (pulselessness, paraesthesia, pallor, paralysis) mean the limb is already in trouble. It is a limb-threatening surgical emergency requiring urgent fasciotomy — do not be reassured by a palpable pulse. Remember an open tibial fracture also needs urgent orthoplastic care.
🎓 Every open tibial fracture needs early antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis and debridement, with severity graded by the Gustilo-Anderson classification and combined orthopaedic-plastic (orthoplastic) management for soft-tissue cover. Always document distal neurovascular status before and after any manipulation.

The ankle is a ring: two malleoli, the talus, and the ligaments that bind them. A single break in the ring often means a second injury somewhere else — so an ankle X-ray is never read as one bone in isolation. First decide who needs the film, then read the mortise for symmetry and classify any fibular fracture by the syndesmosis.

1Decide who gets imaged — Ottawa Ankle Rules
X-ray the ankle only if there is pain in the malleolar zone AND any one of: bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus, bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the medial malleolus, or an inability to weight-bear (four steps) both immediately after injury and in the ED. These rules are highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures and safely reduce unnecessary radiographs.
Tenderness over the navicular or base of 5th metatarsal→apply the Ottawa foot rules and X-ray the foot, not just the ankle
2Get the right views
Standard ankle series is AP, lateral, and mortise. The mortise view is an AP taken with the leg internally rotated ~15–20°, which brings the malleoli into the same plane and profiles the ankle joint (the mortise) so the clear spaces can be compared.
AP — overall alignment, medial clear space, distal tibiofibular overlap.
Lateral — posterior malleolus, talar position, joint effusion, avulsions.
Mortise — symmetry of the medial, superior and lateral clear spaces around the talus.
📷 Image placeholder — mortise view: describe the talus centred in the mortise with equal, uniform clear spaces medially, superiorly and laterally.
3Classify the fibular fracture — Weber
The Weber system grades the lateral malleolus (fibular) fracture by its level relative to the syndesmosis (the distal tibiofibular ligament complex at the plafond). The higher the fracture, the more likely the syndesmosis is torn and the ankle unstable.
AWeber A
Below the syndesmosis. Syndesmosis intact — usually stable, often managed conservatively.
BWeber B
At the level of the syndesmosis. Variable stability — may involve the syndesmosis; check the medial clear space.
CWeber C
Above the syndesmosis. Syndesmosis disrupted — unstable, usually needs surgical fixation.
4Assess the mortise and count the malleoli
On the mortise view the medial, superior and lateral clear spaces should be equal. A widened medial clear space or talar shift means the talus is no longer congruent in the mortise — a sign of deltoid/syndesmotic injury and instability. Remember the ring: a bimalleolar (both malleoli) or trimalleolar fracture (adding the posterior malleolus, best seen on lateral) is unstable by definition.
Medial tenderness, widened medial clear space, but NO lateral malleolus fracture on the ankle film→suspect a Maisonneuve injury — X-ray the whole leg to find a proximal fibula fracture
📷 Image placeholder — mortise view showing an asymmetric, widened medial clear space with the talus shifted laterally; describe the loss of parallelism at the joint.
🚩 An unstable ankle fracture — talar shift, Weber C, bi/trimalleolar, or an open or dislocated ankle with skin tenting or neurovascular compromise — is an orthopaedic emergency. A dislocated ankle should be reduced promptly to protect the skin and neurovascular structures; do not wait for imaging or the on-call team to arrive before relocating a grossly deformed, dusky foot.
🎓 Read every ankle X-ray as a ring: if you see one fracture, actively hunt for the second injury (opposite malleolus, syndesmosis, posterior malleolus, or a high fibula). Symmetry of the mortise clear spaces — not just the presence of a fracture line — is what tells you whether the ankle is stable.

The foot X-ray series (AP/dorsoplantar, oblique and lateral) is the workhorse for midfoot and toe trauma. The oblique view is often the most valuable — it best exposes the base of the 5th metatarsal, the Lisfranc joint alignment and the tarsometatarsal region. Your job is to apply the Ottawa foot rules to decide who needs imaging, then to hunt systematically for the injuries that are famously missed on a quick glance.

1Decide who needs the X-ray — Ottawa foot rules

Image the foot if there is midfoot pain AND any one of: bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal, bony tenderness at the navicular, or an inability to weight-bear (four steps) both immediately and in the department. These rules are highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures and safely reduce unnecessary radiographs.

Midfoot pain + tender 5th MT base or navicular, or can't weight-bear→X-ray foot indicated
2Review systematically (ABCs on every view)

Adequacy and Alignment (smooth arcs at the tarsometatarsal joints), Bone cortices (trace each metatarsal and phalanx), Cartilage/joint spaces, and Soft tissues (swelling, radio-opaque foreign body). Compare the medial borders of the metatarsals and cuneiforms as continuous lines — a step is abnormal.

On the AP/DP view the medial border of the 2nd metatarsal base should line up with the medial border of the middle (intermediate) cuneiform.
On the oblique view the medial border of the 4th metatarsal base should line up with the medial border of the cuboid.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. AP/DP foot showing the normal alignment of the 2nd metatarsal base with the medial edge of the middle cuneiform.
3The 5th metatarsal base — two very different fractures

This is a classic exam trap. Distinguish the location precisely, because prognosis and management differ.

①Pseudo-Jones (avulsion) fracture
Very proximal — an avulsion of the tuberosity from peroneus brevis pull during inversion. Fracture line is usually transverse and does NOT extend into the 4th/5th intermetatarsal joint. Good blood supply → heals well conservatively (supportive footwear, weight-bear as tolerated).
②True Jones fracture
At the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction (roughly 1.5–2 cm distal to the tip of the tuberosity). This is a watershed blood-supply zone → higher risk of delayed/non-union. Often managed with non-weight-bearing cast, and surgical fixation considered in athletes.
Fracture at metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction of 5th MT→Jones — poor blood supply, non-union risk
📷 Image placeholder — describe the radiograph. Oblique foot demonstrating a fracture at the base of the 5th metatarsal; annotate the tuberosity (avulsion zone) versus the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction (Jones zone).
4Lisfranc injury — the one you must not miss

A tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocation, often from an axial load through a plantarflexed foot. Signs are subtle on non-weight-bearing films.

Malalignment of the 2nd metatarsal base with the medial border of the middle cuneiform (loss of the normal continuous line).
A "fleck sign" — a small bony avulsion fragment in the Lisfranc interval (between the medial cuneiform and the 2nd metatarsal base).
Widening of the gap between the 1st and 2nd metatarsal bases.
Fleck sign / step at 2nd MT base / 1st–2nd MT widening→Suspect Lisfranc — get weight-bearing views ± CT
5Don't forget the subtler injuries

March (stress) fracture: classically the 2nd or 3rd metatarsal shaft/neck in soldiers and runners — the initial film may be normal, with periosteal callus only appearing a couple of weeks later. Phalangeal fractures: common from stubbing/crush; check for intra-articular involvement of the great toe. Sesamoid injuries: beneath the 1st MT head — a bipartite sesamoid (smooth margins) can mimic a fracture. Foreign bodies: glass and gravel are radio-opaque — actively look in the soft tissues after a laceration.

🚩 A Lisfranc injury is commonly missed and, if untreated, leads to chronic pain and midfoot arthritis — have a low threshold for weight-bearing views or CT when the mechanism or tenderness fits, even with a "normal" plain film. Likewise, an open fracture or a foot with vascular compromise needs urgent referral. In the diabetic/neuropathic foot, keep osteomyelitis and Charcot arthropathy in mind — the patient may under-report pain despite significant bony destruction.
🎓 "Location is everything" at the 5th metatarsal base: a transverse avulsion of the very tip is a benign pseudo-Jones that heals in comfortable footwear, whereas a fracture 1.5–2 cm distal at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction is a true Jones fracture sitting in a watershed blood-supply zone that risks non-union. Measure before you reassure.

The calcaneus (os calcis) is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone, and the injury has a signature story: a fall from height landing on the heels drives the talus down through the calcaneus in an axial-load pattern. Two views tell you most of it — the lateral (for Böhler's angle) and the axial (Harris) view — but the real exam trick is remembering the injuries above the heel that travel with it.

📷 Image placeholder — lateral ankle/foot radiograph: label the posterior facet of the subtalar joint and mark the two lines used to construct Böhler's angle.
1Know the mechanism before the film
Axial loading of the hindfoot — classically a fall from height onto the heels (roofers, ladders, jumps). The same energy that crushes the calcaneus is transmitted up the skeleton, which is why this is never a "foot only" injury. Most calcaneal fractures (~75%) are intra-articular, involving the subtalar (posterior facet) joint.
2Measure Böhler's angle on the lateral
Böhler's (tuber-joint) angle is formed by a line from the highest point of the posterior tuberosity to the highest point of the posterior facet, and a second line from that facet to the highest point of the anterior process. Normal ≈ 20–40°. A depressed intra-articular fracture flattens the posterior facet, so the angle reduces to <20° — the single most testable radiographic sign. The critical angle of Gissane (normally ~120–145°) sits at the crucial angle beneath the lateral process of the talus and increases when the posterior facet collapses.
Flattened Böhler's angle (<20°)→depressed intra-articular calcaneal fracture until proven otherwise
Lateral view — Böhler's angle and the shape of the posterior facet.
Axial (Harris) view — heel width, varus/valgus alignment, tuberosity extension.
CT (coronal/sagittal) — the true test for articular involvement and surgical planning.
📷 Image placeholder — axial (Harris) view of the calcaneus: describe heel widening and any varus malalignment of the tuberosity fragment.
3Hunt for the injuries above the heel
Axial-load injuries come in patterns. Having found one calcaneal fracture, deliberately look for and exclude the companions:
🦴Contralateral calcaneus
Bilateral fractures are common — always image and examine the opposite heel.
🧬Thoracolumbar spine fracture
~10% have an associated vertebral burst/compression fracture — the classic must-not-miss.
🦵Other lower-limb fractures
Tibial plateau, ankle and hip fractures share the axial-load force.
🩻Pelvic fracture
Higher-energy falls transmit force to the pelvis — examine and image if suspected.
4Mimics and complications
Not every heel pain is a fall-from-height fracture. A calcaneal stress fracture (runners, military recruits) gives normal or subtle early films and a positive squeeze test. An incidental inferior calcaneal spur at the plantar fascia origin is a common finding in plantar fasciitis and is not the cause of acute trauma. After a true fracture, watch for subtalar arthritis, chronic pain, heel widening causing shoe-fitting problems, and — acutely — compartment syndrome of the foot.
🚩 A calcaneal fracture from a fall from height mandates examination and imaging of the spine and the opposite heel/lower limbs — axial-load injuries travel in patterns. Foot compartment syndrome and open fractures need urgent surgical care, and significant intra-articular displacement warrants orthopaedic referral with CT.
🎓 If you learn one number for the OSCE, learn Böhler's angle: normal 20–40°, and a value <20° signals a depressed intra-articular fracture. If you learn one reflex, learn to look up — feel the spine and image the other heel in every heel-strike fall.
PLAIN FILM & FLUOROSCOPY__Fluoroscopy —:
A barium swallow is a real-time fluoroscopic contrast study of the pharynx and oesophagus. The patient swallows a radio-opaque contrast agent while the radiologist watches the bolus pass in real time, capturing spot films at key moments. It is uniquely suited to assessing function (swallowing, peristalsis) as well as structure, making it the go-to test for dysphagia when a motility or structural cause is suspected.

1Why order it — indications

The unifying symptom is trouble getting food down. Key indications:

Dysphagia — difficulty swallowing; the single most common reason.
Odynophagia — painful swallowing.
Suspected stricture — benign (peptic) or malignant.
Suspected pharyngeal pouch (Zenker’s) — regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, gurgling.
Suspected motility disorder — achalasia, diffuse oesophageal spasm.
Suspected perforation or anastomotic leak — but here you must switch contrast (see step 4).
Suspected perforation→Use water-soluble contrast, NOT barium (barium in the mediastinum/peritoneum is inert and causes severe inflammation)
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic study: normal barium swallow, contrast column descending a smooth-walled oesophagus with the GO junction at the diaphragm.
2How it’s performed — technique

The patient stands (or sits) at the fluoroscopy table and swallows barium sulphate suspension on the radiographer’s command while the tube runs in real time. The radiologist watches the bolus live and grabs spot films at key phases.

Single contrast — barium alone; best for demonstrating gross narrowing, motility and the swallowing mechanism.
Double contrast — barium plus effervescent gas granules to distend and coat the wall; best for fine mucosal detail (early tumour, ulcers, webs).
Multiple projections (AP, oblique, lateral) and both erect and prone/semi-recumbent positions are used.
3What you assess

Read the study systematically for four things:

Mucosa — smooth and regular vs ulcerated, nodular or irregular.
Calibre — any narrowing (stricture) or dilatation.
Peristalsis — is the primary wave stripping the bolus normally, or is it absent/uncoordinated?
Gastro-oesophageal (GO) junction — position relative to the diaphragm, opening/relaxation, and any reflux or hernia.
4Key signs & abnormalities

The classic patterns to recognise:

⚠️Malignant stricture
Irregular, “shouldered” narrowing with abrupt mucosal destruction — suspicious for carcinoma.
✅Benign / peptic stricture
Smooth, tapered narrowing at the distal oesophagus, usually from chronic reflux.
💍Schatzki ring
Thin circumferential mucosal ring at the GO junction; intermittent dysphagia to solids.
🕸️Oesophageal web
Thin upper/cervical shelf; with iron-deficiency anaemia & glossitis = Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
👝Pharyngeal pouch
Zenker’s diverticulum — posterior outpouching through Killian’s dehiscence that fills with contrast.
🐦Achalasia
Dilated body tapering to a smooth “bird-beak” at the GO junction; failure of LOS relaxation.
🌀Diffuse oesophageal spasm
Uncoordinated tertiary contractions give a “corkscrew” or rosary-bead appearance.
🔺Hiatus hernia
Stomach herniating above the diaphragm; GO junction/gastric folds seen in the thorax.
🫧Extrinsic compression
Smooth indentation of the contrast column from outside — e.g. mediastinal mass, vascular ring, enlarged left atrium.
Shouldered, irregular stricture→Malignant until proven otherwise — refer for endoscopy & biopsy
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic study: achalasia with a dilated oesophageal body tapering to a smooth “bird-beak” at the GO junction.
🚩 Contrast choice in a nutshell: use barium for the standard study, but if perforation/leak is suspected switch to water-soluble contrast. However, if there is aspiration risk, ionic water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) is dangerous — it draws fluid into the lungs and causes pulmonary oedema. When BOTH perforation and aspiration are a concern, use a non-ionic iso-osmolar agent (e.g. Omnipaque). Barium is also avoided immediately before surgery/CT as residue obscures views.
🎓 Pharyngeal pouch & the NG tube trap: in Zenker’s diverticulum a blindly-passed nasogastric tube can enter and perforate the pouch. If a pouch is known or suspected, NG placement should be done under direct vision or endoscopic/fluoroscopic guidance. Remember the swallow itself carries an aspiration risk and delivers ionising radiation, so gain informed consent and confirm the patient can protect their airway before starting.

The barium (contrast) meal is a fluoroscopic study of the stomach and duodenum. It has been largely superseded by upper GI endoscopy, which visualises the mucosa directly and allows biopsy. It still has a role for assessing gastric outlet and duodenal calibre, defining post-surgical anatomy, and when endoscopy is contraindicated or not tolerated. The modern technique is double-contrast: effervescent granules distend the stomach with gas while a thin, high-density barium coats the mucosa, throwing rugae, ulcers and masses into fine relief.

📷 Image placeholder — double-contrast barium meal showing gas-distended stomach with barium-coated rugal folds.
1Indications & when it is still used

Endoscopy is first-line for dyspepsia, bleeding and suspected malignancy because it permits biopsy. The barium meal retains niche value:

Gastric outlet / duodenal assessment — degree and level of narrowing, gastric emptying.
Post-surgical anatomy — mapping a gastrojejunostomy, Billroth I/II or fundoplication, and checking for leak or obstruction.
Endoscopy contraindicated or failed — unable to intubate, patient intolerance, or a tight stricture the scope cannot pass.
Need mucosal biopsy / tissue diagnosis→Endoscopy, not barium — barium cannot sample tissue
2Technique

The patient is fasted. The study is performed under fluoroscopic screening on a tilting table so the radiologist can position and coat the stomach.

Effervescent granules release CO&sub2; to distend the stomach (the gas component of double-contrast).
High-density barium is swallowed to coat and outline the mucosa for fine detail.
IV Buscopan (hyoscine butylbromide) is given to relax smooth muscle and reduce peristalsis, giving a still, well-distended stomach.
Positioning — the patient is rolled through supine, prone and oblique positions so barium coats all walls and the duodenal cap fills.
🚩 Buscopan is contraindicated in untreated angle-closure glaucoma, and used with caution in significant cardiac disease and prostatic outflow obstruction — it can precipitate acute urinary retention and blurred vision.
3What you assess

Work systematically from oesophagogastric junction to duodenojejunal flexure.

Gastric mucosa & rugae — smooth, evenly coated folds; look for thickening, distortion or effacement.
Ulcers — a barium-filled crater; assess whether it projects beyond the lumen (benign) or lies within it (malignant).
Masses / filling defects — polypoid lesions displacing barium.
Duodenal cap — should be triangular and smoothly outlined; scarring or deformity suggests old ulcer disease.
Gastric outlet — calibre of pylorus and rate of emptying.
4Key signs & abnormalities
🩹Benign gastric ulcer
Crater projects beyond the gastric wall; smooth rolled edge, radiating symmetrical mucosal folds reaching the crater.
⚠️Malignant ulcer
Ulcer lies within the lumen with irregular rolled/heaped edges. Carman meniscus sign — lenticular crater with convex inner margin.
🎗️Gastric carcinoma
Irregular filling defect or ulcerating mass. Diffuse infiltration gives a rigid, non-distensible ‘leather-bottle’ linitis plastica.
🔵Duodenal ulcer
Persistent barium collection in the cap with radiating folds; chronic disease deforms the cap into a ‘trefoil’ shape.
⏳Outlet obstruction
Grossly dilated stomach with retained food/fluid and delayed emptying — from chronic peptic scarring or antral/pyloric tumour.
🔧Post-gastrectomy anatomy
Defines the surgical remnant and anastomosis (Billroth I/II, gastrojejunostomy); look for leak, stenosis or afferent-loop hold-up.
Crater projects OUT beyond the lumen, symmetrical folds→Favours benign; crater WITHIN lumen + heaped edges favours malignant
📷 Image placeholder — barium meal demonstrating linitis plastica with a rigid, narrowed, non-distensible stomach.
🚩 If perforation is suspected, do NOT use barium — extravasated barium causes severe chemical peritonitis. Use a water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) instead. Conversely, if there is significant aspiration risk, Gastrografin is hazardous — it is hyperosmolar and causes severe pulmonary oedema if aspirated, so barium is preferred there. Choose the agent for the specific clinical risk.
🎓 Endoscopy is now first-line for the stomach and duodenum because it both visualises the mucosa directly and allows biopsy — a barium meal can raise the suspicion of malignancy but can never confirm it. Any mass or suspicious ulcer seen on a barium study still needs endoscopic biopsy for tissue diagnosis. Remember it remains a radiation exposure requiring justification and appropriate consent.

The barium follow-through (small bowel follow-through, SBFT) is a timed fluoroscopic study of the small bowel: the patient drinks a barium suspension and sequential films track the column of contrast from the duodenum to the caecum. It remains a cheap, widely available way to assess small bowel calibre, mucosal fold pattern and transit, though CT and MR enterography and capsule endoscopy now often supersede it — particularly for suspected Crohn's disease, where cross-sectional imaging also shows transmural and extramural disease.

1Indications — when the small bowel is the question
Crohn's disease — assessment of terminal ileal and skip disease, strictures and fistulae.
Suspected small bowel obstruction — level and completeness, when CT is equivocal or unavailable.
Malabsorption — coeliac-type fold changes, dilatation, flocculation.
Suspected tumour, diverticula or Meckel's — though yield is lower.
Detailed mucosal or transmural detail needed→prefer CT / MR enterography or capsule endoscopy
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic study: a normal follow-through film with the barium column reaching the caecum and a feathery jejunal fold pattern.
2Technique — drink, time, compress
The patient drinks a dilute barium sulphate suspension (often with an effervescent or prokinetic aid to speed transit).
Sequential timed overhead films are taken (e.g. 15–30 min intervals) as contrast transits, typically until it reaches the caecum — up to a few hours.
Intermittent fluoroscopy with compression (spot) views, especially of the terminal ileum, separate overlapping loops and improve mucosal assessment.
Perforation or high-grade obstruction suspected→use water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) instead of barium
3What you assess
Mucosal fold pattern — feathery valvulae conniventes in jejunum; effaced, thickened or nodular folds suggest disease.
Calibre — normal small bowel < 3 cm; dilatation implies obstruction, ileus or malabsorption.
Transit time — rapid transit in malabsorption; delayed in obstruction.
Terminal ileum — the key target: strictures, ulceration, cobblestoning, separation of loops.
4Key signs & abnormalities
🎗️String sign of Kantor
Thin ribbon of barium through a tight, spasmed / strictured terminal ileum in Crohn's.
🔀Skip lesions
Discontinuous diseased segments with intervening normal bowel — characteristic of Crohn's.
🧱Cobblestoning
Longitudinal & transverse ulcers around oedematous islands of mucosa.
🕳️Fistulae / sinus tracts
Abnormal contrast-filled tracts between loops or to other organs — a Crohn's complication.
🎈Dilatation & obstruction
Dilated proximal loops with a transition point and hold-up of contrast.
🌾Malabsorption pattern
Dilated bowel, thickened / effaced folds, flocculation and dilution of barium.
Diverticula or outpouchings on antimesenteric border→consider small bowel diverticulosis or Meckel's
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic study: a compression spot view of the terminal ileum showing the string sign of Kantor and cobblestone mucosa in Crohn's disease.
🚩 If bowel perforation or a leak is suspected, do NOT use barium — extravasated barium causes a severe granulomatous peritonitis. Use water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin). Conversely, hyperosmolar water-soluble contrast is dangerous if aspirated (can cause pulmonary oedema), so barium is preferred when there is a real aspiration risk and no perforation concern.
🎓 Enteroclysis gives superior mucosal detail because barium (± methylcellulose for a double-contrast effect) is instilled directly through a nasojejunal tube to distend the bowel — but it needs intubation and a higher radiation dose, so the simpler drink-and-follow SBFT remains the everyday compromise.

A water-soluble contrast swallow uses iodinated contrast instead of barium to opacify the pharynx and oesophagus under real-time fluoroscopy. The single teaching point that examiners love: you reach for water-soluble contrast whenever a leak or perforation is suspected, because extravasated barium into the mediastinum or peritoneum triggers a severe, often fatal, chemical inflammatory reaction. The trade-off is that you must then think carefully about which water-soluble agent to use, because ionic hyperosmolar gastrografin is itself dangerous if it enters the lungs.

1Indications — when NOT to use barium

The core decision is driven by whether integrity of the wall is in question. If you suspect the lumen is breached, barium is out.

Suspected oesophageal perforation (e.g. Boerhaave, post-instrumentation)→Water-soluble contrast — barium causes mediastinitis
Post-operative anastomotic leak (post-oesophagectomy, bariatric sleeve/bypass)→Water-soluble swallow to assess anastomotic integrity before feeding
Suspected tracheo-oesophageal fistula→Water-soluble contrast — but NON-ionic if any aspiration risk
Abdominal signs / suspected peritonitis with hollow-viscus breach→Barium into peritoneum causes barium peritonitis — avoid
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic swallow showing a contained collection of extravasated water-soluble contrast tracking outside the oesophageal lumen at an anastomosis.
2Technique

The patient swallows a mouthful of water-soluble iodinated contrast while the radiologist screens the pharynx and oesophagus in real time under fluoroscopy, usually erect and in oblique projections, with spot images captured as contrast passes.

Watch the bolus transit the full length of the oesophagus to the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Look actively for any contrast passing outside the expected lumen — extravasation is the abnormality that defines a leak.
Trace whether contrast enters the airway (aspiration or fistula) or tracks into the mediastinum / a surgical drain.
If no leak is seen with dilute agent but suspicion remains high, the study may be repeated or CT with oral contrast performed.
3Choosing the RIGHT water-soluble agent

Not all water-soluble contrast is equal. Ionic hyperosmolar agents (gastrografin) draw fluid into the airway if aspirated, causing acute pulmonary oedema and chemical pneumonitis that can be life-threatening. So the safe agent depends on the risk profile.

🥛Barium
Best mucosal detail — use when leak is NOT suspected. Contraindicated if perforation/leak possible (mediastinitis, barium peritonitis).
⚠️Ionic (gastrografin)
Hyperosmolar. Safe if it leaks into mediastinum/peritoneum. DANGEROUS if aspirated — causes pulmonary oedema. Use only when leak suspected AND aspiration risk is low.
✅Non-ionic low-osmolar
Safe in the airway AND safe if it leaks. The compromise agent when BOTH perforation and aspiration risk coexist (e.g. suspected TOF, unsafe swallow).
Leak suspected + aspiration risk (frail, reduced GCS, TOF)→Low-osmolar NON-ionic iodinated contrast
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic study showing contrast passing from the oesophagus into the trachea, indicating a tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
4Signs & safety
Contrast extravasation / leak: contrast escaping the lumen into the mediastinum, neck, peritoneum or a drain confirms perforation or anastomotic breakdown.
Fistula: an abnormal track of contrast into the airway (tracheo-oesophageal) or another viscus.
Consent covers the small radiation dose and the rationale for the chosen contrast agent; use ALARA principles and keep screening time short.
🚩 NEVER give ionic hyperosmolar gastrografin when there is any aspiration risk — if it enters the lungs it causes acute pulmonary oedema and chemical pneumonitis. If aspiration risk is present, use low-osmolar non-ionic iodinated contrast instead.
🚩 NEVER use barium when a leak or perforation is suspected — extravasated barium causes fatal mediastinitis or barium peritonitis.
🎓 Two competing dangers, one safe answer: barium is the enemy of a suspected leak, and hyperosmolar gastrografin is the enemy of the lungs. When BOTH perforation and aspiration are in play, low-osmolar non-ionic iodinated contrast is the compromise that is safe in the mediastinum and safe in the airway.

Videofluoroscopy (videofluoroscopic swallow study, VFSS — also called the modified barium swallow) is a real-time fluoroscopic recording of a patient swallowing barium-coated food and fluid of different consistencies. It is performed jointly with a speech and language therapist (SALT) and is the reference-standard functional assessment of oropharyngeal dysphagia and aspiration risk. Unlike a barium swallow, the question is not anatomy but safety: does the airway stay protected?

📷 Image placeholder — lateral fluoroscopic still of the oropharynx during a swallow, annotated to show the vallecula, piriform fossae, laryngeal vestibule and the level of the vocal cords.
1Indications — who needs it

Requested when there is clinical concern about oropharyngeal dysphagia and aspiration, typically after a failed or equivocal bedside swallow assessment.

Stroke with coughing on drinking→assess safe consistencies before oral feeding resumes
Progressive neurological disease (MND, Parkinson’s, MS)→quantify aspiration risk, guide long-term feeding plan
Head & neck cancer / post-surgery or radiotherapy→map altered swallow, residue and penetration
2Technique — how it is done

The patient sits upright and is given a range of barium-coated consistencies by the SALT while the radiologist screens and records the swallow as video, so the phases can be reviewed frame by frame in real time.

Consistencies tested: thin fluid → thickened fluid → puree → solid.
Views: lateral screening (best for airway and the phases) plus AP to check for asymmetry between the two piriform fossae.
Team: performed with a speech and language therapist who directs consistencies, positioning and compensatory manoeuvres.
3What you assess

The swallow is analysed in phases, looking specifically for the point at which the airway is threatened.

👅Oral phase
Bolus formation and control; oral residue, premature spill over the tongue base.
🗣️Pharyngeal phase
Timing and strength of the swallow reflex, laryngeal elevation, cricopharyngeal opening.
⚠️Penetration
Contrast enters the laryngeal vestibule but stays above the vocal cords.
🔻Aspiration
Contrast passes below the vocal cords into the trachea — frank aspiration.
🥄Residue
Pooling in the valleculae and piriform fossae after the swallow — a source of post-swallow aspiration.
🤫Silent aspiration
Contrast below the cords with no cough — the most dangerous finding, missed at the bedside.
🚩 Silent aspiration — aspiration with no protective cough — is invisible on a bedside swallow screen and is a key reason to request videofluoroscopy. It carries a high risk of aspiration pneumonia.
📷 Image placeholder — sequential frames showing contrast tracking into the laryngeal vestibule and passing below the vocal cords, illustrating penetration versus frank aspiration.
4Outcome, safety & FEES

The joint report guides real clinical decisions with the SALT.

Guides safe consistencies (e.g. thickened fluids, puree diet) and compensatory manoeuvres.
Decides feeding route — if the swallow is unsafe, recommends NG (short-term) or PEG (long-term) feeding.
Directs swallow rehabilitation and monitors progress over time.

Safety: there is a risk of aspirating contrast, so appropriate contrast is used (barium is inert if aspirated in small amounts, but low/iso-osmolar water-soluble agents are preferred where large-volume aspiration is likely; high-osmolar agents such as gastrografin are avoided as they cause pulmonary oedema if aspirated). The study carries a radiation dose, so screening time is kept short. Remember this is a functional, not an anatomical study.

🎓 VFSS vs FEES: Fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) uses a nasendoscope to view the pharynx and larynx directly — no radiation, can be done at the bedside, and gives excellent views of secretions and residue, but has a ‘white-out’ blind spot at the moment of the swallow. VFSS sees the whole swallow including the oral phase and cricopharyngeus but uses radiation. They are complementary.

Small bowel enema (enteroclysis) is a dedicated, high-detail fluoroscopic examination of the small bowel mucosa. Contrast is infused directly into the proximal jejunum through a naso-jejunal tube, giving controlled distension and double-contrast mucosal detail that the ordinary oral barium follow-through cannot match. It answers a focused question — what does the small bowel wall and lumen actually look like — in the small number of patients where cross-sectional imaging has not settled things. In modern UK practice MR and CT enterography have largely displaced it, but it remains an examinable technique and is still used where fine mucosal or fold detail is decisive.

📷 Image placeholder — naso-jejunal tube with tip beyond the duodeno-jejunal flexure, contrast filling distended jejunal loops.
1Why order it — indications

Enteroclysis is reserved for problems needing dedicated, high-resolution mucosal assessment of the small bowel, typically when other modalities are equivocal.

Suspected low-grade / intermittent small bowel obstruction→Distension unmasks a subtle transition point or adhesive band not seen on follow-through
Crohn's disease — extent and mucosal detail→Skip lesions, early aphthous change, strictures and fistulae
Small bowel tumour or polyp / obscure GI bleeding→Search for a filling defect or mucosal lesion when endoscopy and CT are negative

Note: MR enterography (no radiation, excellent wall/extramural detail) and CT enterography are now often preferred, so enteroclysis is a second-line, problem-solving study.

2How it is performed — technique
A naso-jejunal (NJ) tube is passed and advanced under fluoroscopic guidance until the tip lies beyond the duodeno-jejunal (DJ) flexure — this bypasses the stomach and pylorus so infusion rate is controlled by the radiologist, not gastric emptying.
Barium is infused first to coat and outline the mucosa (single-contrast phase).
Then methylcellulose (or air) is infused to push the barium onwards and distend the loops — the low-density methylcellulose column stretches the bowel and produces the double-contrast effect, giving superior mucosal and fold detail.
Compression and spot fluoroscopic images are taken of each segment as loops fill and distend; screening continues to the terminal ileum.

Water-soluble contrast (e.g. gadolinium for MR, or iodinated agent) is substituted for barium if there is any suspicion of perforation or a planned early operation.

3What you assess — and enteroclysis vs follow-through
Fold pattern: normal feathery valvulae conniventes vs effacement, thickening or fold distortion.
Strictures & dilatation: luminal narrowing, proximal dilatation and any transition point.
Masses / filling defects: polyps, tumours, intraluminal or mural lesions.
Terminal ileum: the classic site for Crohn's — look for narrowing, ulceration and nodularity.

Enteroclysis vs barium follow-through: enteroclysis gives better distension and mucosal detail because contrast is delivered directly and the loops are actively stretched — but it is invasive (NJ intubation), less comfortable and less physiological. The oral follow-through is simpler and better tolerated but relies on gastric emptying and gives poorer, variable distension.

📷 Image placeholder — double-contrast enteroclysis showing a distended jejunum with a smooth stricture and proximal dilatation.
4Key signs & abnormalities
🌿Crohn's strictures
Long narrowed segment ("string sign") with skip lesions between normal bowel
🔀Fistulae
Abnormal tracks of contrast between loops or to skin/other organs in Crohn's
⚪Tumours / polyps
Rounded intraluminal filling defects; may cause obstruction or intussusception
🪢Adhesions
Angulation, fixation and a transition point of loops without a mucosal mass
🚩 Substitute water-soluble contrast for barium if perforation is possible — extravasated barium into the peritoneum causes a severe granulomatous peritonitis. Guard the airway: aspiration of contrast during NJ intubation is a real risk, especially in obstruction or impaired swallow.
🎓 The whole point of the naso-jejunal tube and methylcellulose is controlled distension: by delivering contrast past the DJ flexure the radiologist stretches the loops actively, so subtle strictures and fold changes that collapse on a follow-through are held open and revealed.

The barium/contrast enema is a fluoroscopic study of the large bowel, in which contrast is instilled per rectum to opacify the colon from rectum to caecum. For elective mucosal assessment it has now been largely superseded by colonoscopy (which also biopsies and removes polyps) and CT colonography. It retains an important role in specific situations, and the water-soluble contrast enema in particular remains a key acute investigation for suspected obstruction, volvulus, intussusception and anastomotic integrity.

1Indications & when it is still used

Elective luminal/mucosal assessment of the colon is now first-line by colonoscopy or CT colonography, so the classic double-contrast barium enema is requested far less than before. Contrast enema persists where endoscopy is incomplete, contraindicated, declined or unavailable, and the water-soluble study is genuinely important in the acute setting.

Elective (barium): incomplete/failed colonoscopy, assessment of stricture length, characterisation of diverticular disease.
Acute (water-soluble): suspected large bowel obstruction, sigmoid volvulus, suspected intussusception, and post-operative anastomotic leak check.
Mucosal detail & polyps needed→colonoscopy / CT colonography, not barium
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic study: double-contrast barium enema with barium coating the mucosa and air distending the colonic loops.
2Technique — double vs single contrast

The contrast medium and technique are chosen for the clinical question. Double-contrast barium enema gives the best mucosal detail; a single-contrast/water-soluble study is used where perforation, leak or obstruction is a concern.

Double-contrast barium: bowel prep (laxatives + low-residue diet) to empty the colon → rectal catheter → barium run in, then insufflated with air to distend and thin the barium into a mucosal coat → IV Buscopan (hyoscine butylbromide) to reduce spasm → imaged in multiple positions (supine, prone, decubitus, erect) to move contrast/air through all segments.
Single-contrast / water-soluble (Gastrografin): water-soluble iodinated contrast without air; used for suspected obstruction, volvulus, intussusception, and anastomotic leak, where any extravasation is safely resorbed.
Perforation / leak possible→water-soluble contrast, never barium
3What you assess

Systematically follow the contrast column from rectum to caecum, assessing the lumen and mucosal outline in each segment.

Mucosa: smooth vs ulcerated/granular; loss of the normal haustral pattern.
Strictures: length, symmetry and margins (smooth benign vs shouldered malignant).
Filling defects: polyps, tumours, or in acute reduction a soft-tissue mass (intussusceptum).
Diverticula: outpouchings, especially sigmoid; associated muscle spasm/deformity.
4Key signs & acute applications

Recognise the classic appearances and the acute problems the water-soluble enema answers.

Short shouldered irregular stricture→colorectal carcinoma (apple-core / napkin-ring)
Smooth tubular colon, no haustra→chronic ulcerative colitis (lead-pipe colon)
Bird-beak taper at rectosigmoid, no proximal filling→sigmoid volvulus
Contrast reaches caecum freely, dilated colon→pseudo-obstruction rather than mechanical block

Acute uses of the water-soluble contrast enema:

Large bowel obstruction: confirms a mechanical transition point and distinguishes true obstruction from pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie), where contrast passes freely to a dilated caecum.
Sigmoid volvulus: demonstrates the bird-beak/tapered point of torsion.
Intussusception (children): air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic — hydrostatic/pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopic control.
Anastomotic leak check: water-soluble enema post colorectal surgery to confirm integrity before restoring oral intake or reversing a stoma.
🍎Colorectal carcinoma
Apple-core / napkin-ring: short, shouldered, irregular annular stricture with abrupt margins.
🕳️Diverticular disease
Multiple sigmoid outpouchings, luminal narrowing and a serrated/saw-tooth muscle spasm pattern.
🔘Polyps
Rounded filling defects, sessile or pedunculated; refer for colonoscopy to biopsy/remove.
🚰Colitis (UC)
Loss of haustra with a smooth featureless lead-pipe colon; granular ulcerated mucosa.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluoroscopic study: single-contrast water-soluble enema showing a bird-beak taper at the rectosigmoid junction in sigmoid volvulus.
🚩 Barium enema is CONTRAINDICATED where perforation is suspected, in toxic megacolon, and after recent deep/hot biopsy — extravasated barium causes severe chemical peritonitis. Use a water-soluble agent instead. The risk of iatrogenic perforation is highest in the acute or inflamed colon, so insufflate cautiously and take informed consent covering perforation, discomfort/bloating and Buscopan effects (blurred vision, dry mouth, urinary retention; avoid in angle-closure glaucoma).
🎓 A free flow of water-soluble contrast all the way to a dilated caecum with no mechanical transition point points to pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) rather than mechanical large bowel obstruction — a distinction that changes management from theatre to conservative/decompressive treatment.

The defecating proctogram (evacuation proctography, or defecography) is a dynamic functional fluoroscopic study of the anorectum and pelvic floor during simulated defecation. Unlike a static contrast enema that maps anatomy, it films the rectum in the act of emptying — capturing how the anorectal angle, pelvic floor and rectal wall behave at rest, on squeeze, on cough and during active straining and evacuation. It is the workhorse investigation for obstructed defecation and pelvic floor dysfunction.

1Why it is requested
Referrals come chiefly from colorectal surgery and pelvic floor clinics for symptoms that structural imaging cannot explain. It is frequently the deciding test before pelvic floor surgery.
Obstructed defecation — straining, incomplete emptying, sense of blockage, digitation.
Faecal incontinence — to characterise pelvic floor and anorectal angle behaviour.
Suspected rectocele, enterocele, intussusception or rectal prolapse.
Pelvic floor dysfunction — and pre-operative workup before pelvic floor / prolapse surgery.
Patient strains hard yet cannot empty→Think obstructed defecation — proctogram to distinguish mechanical (rectocele/intussusception) from functional (anismus) cause
2How the study is performed
A thick barium paste (stiff, stool-consistency contrast) is introduced into the rectum to mimic faeces. Additional compartments may be opacified to unmask multi-compartment pathology: vaginal contrast/gel, oral contrast to opacify small bowel (to reveal an enterocele), and occasionally the bladder. The patient is seated on a radiolucent commode, and lateral fluoroscopy is recorded through a defined sequence:
Rest — baseline anorectal angle and pelvic floor position.
Squeeze — voluntary contraction; the angle should sharpen (puborectalis pulls the rectum forward).
Cough — tests pelvic floor competence and unmasks prolapse.
Evacuation / strain — the key phase; the patient actively empties while the emptying is filmed.

3What you assess
Reading is dynamic — you compare phases, not a single frame.
Anorectal angle — should sharpen (close) on squeeze and open (widen) on strain to allow evacuation.
Pelvic floor descent — degree of perineal/pelvic floor lowering from rest to strain.
Evacuation — completeness and speed of emptying, and any contrast trapping.
Anal canal — opening and calibre during evacuation.
Anorectal angle fails to open (stays acute) on straining→Non-relaxing pelvic floor — anismus / paradoxical puborectalis contraction
4Key abnormalities and signs
The commonest findings cluster into mechanical outlet problems and functional (pelvic floor) problems.
👝Rectocele
Anterior bulging of the rectal wall into the vagina; contrast is trapped in the bulge and empties late/incompletely.
🎈Enterocele
Small bowel loops descending into the rectovaginal space — best seen with small-bowel opacification.
🌀Intussusception
Rectal wall infolding (internal intussusception) during evacuation; may progress to prolapse.
⬇️Rectal prolapse
Full-thickness rectal wall protruding through the anus externally on straining.
🚫Anismus
Paradoxical puborectalis contraction — anorectal angle fails to open, non-relaxing pelvic floor, prolonged/failed evacuation.
📉Excess descent
Excessive perineal descent — abnormal lowering of the pelvic floor on strain (descending perineum syndrome).

🚩 This is a functional, not purely structural, study — the diagnosis lives in how the anorectum moves across the phases. A single static frame can miss anismus, dynamic intussusception or a rectocele that only trap contrast on active evacuation. Always interpret the evacuation sequence as a whole.
🎓 MR defecography is a radiation-free alternative that adds superb soft-tissue and multi-compartment detail (bladder, uterus, all three pelvic compartments) — increasingly favoured, especially in younger women. Because conventional proctography delivers a meaningful radiation dose to the pelvis and gonads, it must be justified in women of reproductive age; consider MR where available. Throughout, guard patient dignity and informed consent — evacuating on a commode under fluoroscopy is understandably distressing, so a calm, private environment and clear explanation are essential.
